new_statements.quote: Der Akzent liegt, wie im Ali, im allgemeinen auf der letzten Silbe, wenn das Wort auf zwei Vokale endigt, auf der vorletzten; ebenso liegt bei den Possessivformen der Akzent stets auf der vorletzten Silbe.
new_statements.translation: The accent lies, as in Ali, in general on the last syllable; when the word ends in two vowels, on the penultimate; likewise in the possessive forms the accent always lies on the penultimate syllable.
new_statements.citation: Klaffl, Johann & Friedrich Vormann (mit Zusätzen von P. W. Schmidt). 1905. Die Sprachen des Berlinhafen-Bezirks in Deutsch-Neuguinea. Mitteilungen des Seminars für Orientalische Sprachen zu Berlin 8 (Abt. I): 1-138. Berlin: Reichsdruckerei. [Tumleo section by P. Joh. Klaffl, S.V.D.]
new_statements.locator: p. 52, '4. Die Tumleo-Sprache', I. Grammatik, § 70 'B. Lautverhältnisse' (PDF page 60 of the archive.org scan bub_gb_eYhBAAAAYAAJ)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote verified on the saved page scan (printed p. 52 = PDF page 60 of): under "4. Die Tumleo-Sprache. Von P. Joh. Klaffl, S.V.D.", I. Grammatik, §70 B. Lautverhältnisse, the sentence reads exactly "Der Akzent liegt, wie im Ali, im allgemeinen auf der letzten Silbe, wenn das Wort auf zwei Vokale endigt, auf der vorletzten; ebenso liegt bei den Possessivformen der Akzent stets auf der vorletzten Silbe." The extracted text (line 3709-3711) has scanned slips "hegt" and "Possessivfornien"; the image is unambiguous. Identity: §69 on the same page, "Die Insel Tumleo, Berlinhafen. Die Sprache wird von nur etwa 300 Menschen gesprochen.. der Ali-Sprache verwandt" - Tumleo Island proper, i.e. tuml1238…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent falls by default on the final syllable. Two stated exceptions: words ending in a sequence of two vowels are stressed on the penult (i.e. on the first of the two final vowels, as the parallel Ali rule on p. 3 makes explicit), and possessive-suffixed forms are always stressed on the penult. Ross 1988: 86 adds, from Schultze 1911's data, that in some verbs stress alternates morphologically: root-final in 1S/2S (na-ús, ka-ús) but on the subject prefix in the other persons (ká-us, tá-us, rá-us).
new_statements.exceptions: (1) words ending in two vowels: penult; (2) possessive forms (noun + possessive suffix): always penult; (3) per Ross 1988: 85-86 citing Schultze 1911: 17-21, a person-conditioned stress alternation in some verbs (1S/2S stress the root, other persons stress the prefix).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('das Wort'); based on an early missionary description (Klaffl, SVD) written from the Ali grammar as template ('wie im Ali'); no instrumental data; c. 300 speakers on Tumleo Island at the time. The Ali comparison on p. 3 also describes accent on the first of two final vowels ('so hat der erstere den Ton').
new_statements.identity_note: The statement is for the Tumleo language of Tumleo Island proper (Klaffl 1905 §69: 'Die Insel Tumleo, Berlinhafen', c. 300 speakers), i.e. tuml1238 itself; Klaffl frames it against Ali (alii1246, 'wie im Ali'), whose own rule on p. 3 is the same final-stress pattern with penult in possessive forms. Ross 1988's verb-stress paradigm is also labelled Tumleo (ultimately from Schultze 1911).

new_statements.quote: Alók heißt z. B. hier eine Frau, in Leming heißt so ein Junge, allerdings mit der dem dortigen Sprachgeiste entsprechenden Betonung álok. [...] 16. Lapói (i schwach), heißt in Leming »groß«. In Leming liegt dem Geiste der Sprache nach der Ton auf der paenultima. [...] 24. Eiló, Name des Flusses Rajú, nördlich von Leming bei den dortigen Leuten, die aber Eílo betonen.
new_statements.translation: Alók, for example, is the name of a woman here; in Leming it is the name of a boy, but with the accentuation álok that corresponds to the spirit of the language there. [...] 16. Lapói (i weak) means 'big' in Leming. In Leming, according to the spirit of the language, the stress lies on the penult. [...] 24. Eiló, name of the river Rajú, north of Leming among the people there, who however stress it Eílo.
new_statements.citation: Erdweg, Mathias Josef. 1902. Die Bewohner der Insel Tumleo, Berlinhafen, Deutsch-Neu-Guinea. Mitteilungen der Anthropologischen Gesellschaft in Wien 32: 274-399.
new_statements.locator: p. 388 (IAI scan page 118), list of school-children's names, introductory paragraph and items 16 and 24; verified on the page scan (the scanned drops the acute accents)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (printed p. 388) and from Erdweg_1902_Bewohner_Tumleo_IAI_plaintext.zip. All three quoted passages are verbatim on the page scan: 'Alók heißt z. B. hier eine Frau, in Leming heißt so ein Junge, allerdings mit der dem dortigen Sprachgeiste entsprechenden Betonung álok.' (lines 12-13 of the introductory paragraph); '16. Lapói (i schwach), heißt in Leming »groß«. In Leming liegt dem Geiste der Sprache nach der Ton auf der paenultima.'; '24. Eiló, Name des Flusses Rajú, nördlich von Leming bei den dortigen Leuten, die aber Eílo betonen.' The scanned drops the acutes ('Alök.. «lok', 'Zapoi (Üschwach)', 'Eilö.. Eilo'), exactly as the compiler said. I checked every accent on the page scan:…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with Klaffl 1905: 52 §70 (general final stress, penult when the word ends in two vowels): the accented Tumleo names and the explicit contrast with Leming penult stress point the same way, but Erdweg never states a Tumleo rule, so this is incidental corroboration rather than an independent statement. The Leming remark is about another (mainland) language, not Tumleo.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Erdweg is an ethnography with no grammar or sound section and states no stress rule for Tumleo itself. The only explicit rule is for the neighbouring mainland village language Leming (penultimate stress), given as a contrast to Tumleo: the Tumleo forms Alók, Lapói, Eiló are final-stressed where Leming has álok, Eílo. The accent marks he places on the Tumleo names of the page are almost all on the last syllable (Alók, Lamaanén, anén, Umpó, Mōskanjún, kankanán, Anjí, Auvijáret, Arét, Masón, Alapón, Arakól, Eijrerór, Panáh, Apó, apú, Simél, Paniweí, Savaú, Eiló, Rajú), with penult accent in Láma 'person', Vúi, Tjaméo, Sírma. So the work implicitly supports final stress for Tumleo, with penult stress in a word ending in two vowels (Tjaméo) exactly as Klaffl's rule predicts.
new_statements.exceptions: Only implicit: penult-accented names Láma, Vúi, Tjaméo, Sírma among the final-accented majority; Tjaméo fits Klaffl's two-final-vowels clause.
new_statements.identity_note: Erdweg 1902 describes Tumleo Island (Berlinhafen), the same variety as Klaffl 1905 §69 (c. 300 speakers) = tuml1238; his explicit stress rule ('Ton auf der paenultima') concerns Leming, a neighbouring mainland village language, and is quoted only as a contrast with Tumleo. Names glossed from Arop, Sel&o (Seleo) and Leming are other Schouten varieties.

sources.note: §70 'B. Lautverhältnisse', p. 52: accent generally on the last syllable, as in Ali; on the penult when the word ends in two vowels; always on the penult in possessive forms. Ali section §3, p. 3, gives the parallel rule for Ali (final; penult in possessive forms and in adjectives intensified with -plä; first of two final vowels bears the tone). No other accent remark in the Tumleo section; the Tumleo vocabulary is not accent-marked.
